nameStory: Cutleaf deadnettle gets its name from its deeply divided, "cut" leaves that look like they've been snipped with scissors. The "deadnettle" part comes from its resemblance to stinging nettle, but without the sting - hence "dead" or harmless nettle. Despite the intimidating name, this little plant is completely safe to touch!
description: Cutleaf deadnettle is a small, low-growing annual herb that rarely reaches more than 8-10 inches tall. It's a member of the mint family with square stems and deeply lobed leaves that give it a delicate, lacy appearance. The plant produces small pinkish-purple flowers clustered near the top and has a somewhat sprawling growth habit, often forming small patches in disturbed soil.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are deeply cut or lobed, almost feathery-looking, with much more dramatic divisions than other deadnettles. The upper leaves often have a purplish tinge, and they feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pinkish-purple flowers cluster in whorls near the stem tips, typical of mint family plants. Each flower has the characteristic two-lipped shape with a hooded upper lip.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading annual that stays close to the ground, often forming small colonies. The square stems are typical of mint family plants and feel slightly ridged when rolled between your fingers.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Four-sided square stems that are often reddish or purplish, especially at the joints where leaves attach. The stems feel hollow and somewhat brittle when bent.

habitat: Look for cutleaf deadnettle in disturbed soils like garden beds, roadsides, waste areas, and cultivated ground throughout New England. It thrives in rich, moist soil and partial shade but can tolerate full sun. Often found alongside other weedy species in areas where the soil has been recently turned or disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge early and begin flowering by late spring. This is when the deeply cut leaves are most distinctive and the plant is easiest to identify.
seasonality.summer: Continues flowering through early summer, though plants may struggle in hot, dry conditions. Seeds are forming and dispersing by mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: Annual plants die back after setting seed. Look for dried brown stems and seed remnants in areas where it grew earlier in the year.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent as this is an annual plant. Seeds lie dormant in the soil waiting for spring warmth to germinate.

funFact: Despite being called a "deadnettle," this plant is actually edible and has been used in traditional European cooking - the young leaves can be added to salads or cooked like spinach, with a mild, slightly minty flavor!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with red deadnettle and henbit deadnettle, but cutleaf deadnettle's leaves are much more deeply divided - think "deeply cut" versus "scalloped edges." Memory trick: cutleaf looks like someone took scissors to the leaves, while the others just look gently wavy.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name "hybridum" means "hybrid," though this isn't actually a hybrid species - the botanist who named it never explained why he chose this confusing name. Don't let the name fool you into thinking it's a cross between other species!
compareHints: Among the deadnettles, cutleaf deadnettle stands out for its dramatically dissected leaves - much more deeply cut than red deadnettle's heart-shaped leaves or henbit's rounded, scalloped ones. While red deadnettle has leaves that clasp the stem and henbit has leaves that completely encircle it, cutleaf deadnettle's leaves attach with distinct petioles (leaf stalks). The overall plant also tends to be more delicate and lacy-looking than its chunkier relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red deadnettle differs from other Lamium species by its stalked, triangular-heart-shaped leaves and consistent purple-pink flower color.
Among the deadnettles, henbit is unique for its stem-clasping upper leaves - red deadnettle has all stalked leaves, while white and spotted deadnettles are much larger perennial plants.

Yellow archangel stands out from its deadnettle relatives primarily by its golden flowers - red deadnettle has pink-purple blooms, henbit has smaller purple flowers, and white deadnettle has white flowers.
Among its deadnettle relatives, spotted deadnettle is the only one with distinctive silvery-white leaf markings - red deadnettle and henbit have plain green leaves.
White deadnettle stands out from its relatives by its pure white flowers and perennial growth habit.
